title: The level of overall economic activity

questions.prompt: In a simple two-sector circular flow model, what do households provide to firms, and what do they receive in return?
hints: Use the circular flow of income with its factor (resource) market and product market.
Follow the flows from households to firms in the factor market, and then the flow that comes back.
questions.targets: Real and money flows in the two-sector circular flow

options.text: Factors of production, in exchange for incomes such as wages, rent, interest and profit
Goods and services, in exchange for consumer spending
options.misconception: Goods and services do flow in the model, but firms provide them to households, not the other way round.

options.text: Consumer spending, in exchange for factors of production
options.misconception: Households do spend, but spending buys goods and services, not factors of production.

options.text: Savings, in exchange for investment goods
options.misconception: Saving and investment appear in the wider model, but they are not part of the simple two-sector flow.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a leakage and an injection in the circular flow of income, giving one example of each.
hints: Use the open-economy circular flow model with the financial, government and foreign sectors.
For each term, describe what it does to the size of the flow of spending and name one matching example.
questions.targets: Leakages vs injections with examples
marking_points: A leakage (withdrawal) is income taken out of the circular flow and not spent on domestic output, e.g. saving, taxes or imports [1]
An injection is spending added to the circular flow that does not come from household consumption, e.g. investment, government spending or exports [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer contrasts money leaving the flow with money entering it, with a correct example of each.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an injection into Veld's circular flow of income?
hints: Use the three leakages and three injections of the open-economy circular flow.
Ask whether each flow removes money from, or adds money to, spending on Veld's output.
questions.targets: Classifying injections and leakages

options.text: Saving by Veld's households
options.misconception: Saved money goes to banks, but it is income that is not spent, so it is a leakage.

options.text: Taxes paid to Veld's government
options.misconception: The government later spends, but paying tax removes income from the flow.

options.text: Spending by Veld's households on imports
options.misconception: This is spending, but the money goes to producers abroad, so it leaks out.

options.text: Spending by foreigners on Veld's exports

questions.prompt: Households in Veld decide to save a larger share of their income. Using the circular flow model, explain how this could affect the level of economic activity.
hints: Use leakages and injections, and the condition for the circular flow to stay the same size.
Trace what happens to spending, then to firms' output and incomes, and consider whether any injection could offset the change.
questions.targets: Effect of a rise in a leakage on the circular flow
marking_points: Saving is a leakage from the circular flow [1]
Higher saving means less consumption spending on domestic output, so firms' revenues fall [1]
Unless injections such as investment rise by the same amount, output, income and employment fall (the flow shrinks) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer identifies saving as a leakage, links it to lower consumption and output, and notes the offset from injections.

questions.prompt: Define the term gross domestic product (GDP).
hints: Think about how the size of a country's national output is measured.
Your answer needs to cover what is counted, where it is produced, and over what period.
questions.targets: Precise definition of GDP
marking_points: The total market value of all final goods and services [1]
produced within a country's borders in a given time period, usually one year [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer mentions the value of final goods and services, production within the country, and a time period.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would be included in Kuva's GDP?
hints: Use the expenditure approach and what counts as spending on final goods and services produced this year.
For each option, ask whether any new output has been produced in this period.
questions.targets: What counts in GDP

options.text: A household buys a second-hand car from a neighbour
options.misconception: Money is spent, but the car was already counted in the year it was produced.

options.text: The government pays pensions to retired people
options.misconception: Government spending is part of GDP, but pensions are transfer payments with no output in return.

options.text: A Kuva firm buys new machinery made in Kuva
A resident buys shares in a Kuva company
options.misconception: It sounds like investment, but buying shares is a financial transaction, not spending on new capital goods.

questions.prompt: Why do economists use real GDP rather than nominal GDP when comparing a country's output over time?
hints: Use the difference between nominal value and real value.
Think about what could make nominal GDP rise even when the quantity of output has not changed.
questions.targets: Purpose of real values

options.text: Real GDP includes the value of intermediate goods
options.misconception: It sounds more complete, but neither measure counts intermediate goods.

options.text: Real GDP removes the effect of changes in the price level
Real GDP divides output by the population
options.misconception: This describes a per capita figure, which is a different adjustment.

options.text: Real GDP is measured in the prices of the current year
options.misconception: Using current prices is exactly what makes a figure nominal.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between gross domestic product (GDP) and gross national income (GNI).
hints: Compare the two measures in terms of where production happens versus who owns the factors of production.
State what each measure counts, and show how one can be found from the other.
questions.targets: GDP vs GNI: location vs ownership
marking_points: GDP measures the value of output produced within a country's borders, whoever owns the factors of production [1]
GNI measures the income earned by a country's residents wherever they produce it, i.e. GDP plus net income from abroad [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer contrasts domestic location (GDP) with residents' income (GNI) and links them through net income from abroad.

questions.prompt: In Tarn, real GDP rises by 3% in a year while the population rises by 5%. What happens to real GDP per capita?
hints: Use the per capita measure: a total divided by the population.
Compare how fast the top of the fraction grows with how fast the bottom grows.
questions.targets: Population growth and GDP per capita

options.text: It falls
It rises by 3%
options.misconception: Real GDP rose by 3%, but that output is now shared among more people.

options.text: It rises by 8%
options.misconception: This adds the two growth rates, but population growth reduces output per person.

options.text: It stays the same, because real GDP rose
options.misconception: Both totals rose, but at different rates, so output per person changes.

questions.prompt: Using Table 1, calculate Veld's GDP using the expenditure method.
hints: Use the expenditure formula, and check which rows are spending on output.
Add the domestic spending components, then add net exports; leave out any item that is not spending on output.
questions.targets: Expenditure method, ignoring a distractor item
marking_points: = 650 billion zed [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer uses C + I + G + (X − M), excludes household saving, and reaches 650 billion zed.

questions.prompt: Using Table 2, what was the value of Kuva's imports?
hints: Use GDP = C + I + G + (X − M) and rearrange it.
Add the known spending items including exports, then compare that total with GDP.
questions.targets: Finding a missing component of expenditure GDP

table.caption: Table 2: National income data for Kuva, 2025

options.text: 870 billion zed
options.misconception: This is C + I + G + X before imports are subtracted, not the value of imports.

options.text: 120 billion zed
options.misconception: This is the export figure; imports are not given and must be calculated.

options.text: 50 billion zed
options.misconception: 800 − 500 − 100 − 150 = 50 gives net exports (X − M), not imports.

options.text: 70 billion zed

questions.prompt: Using Table 3, calculate Tarn's net income from abroad and its gross national income (GNI).
hints: Use the link between GDP and GNI through net income from abroad.
First find the difference between income flowing in and income flowing out, then adjust GDP by that amount, watching the sign.
questions.targets: Net income from abroad and GNI

table.caption: Table 3: Income data for Tarn, 2025
rows: Income earned abroad by Tarn's residents
Income earned in Tarn by foreign-owned factors and sent abroad

marking_points: Net income from abroad = 60 − 85 = −25 million zed [1]
GNI = GDP + net income from abroad = 900 + (−25) [1]
= 875 million zed [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer finds a negative net income from abroad of 25 million zed and a GNI of 875 million zed.

questions.prompt: Using Table 4, what is Veld's GDP deflator for 2025 (base year = 100)?
hints: Use the relationship between nominal GDP, real GDP and the price deflator.
Divide the figures in the correct order and express the result with the base year set at 100.
questions.targets: Calculating the GDP deflator

options.misconception: This divides real GDP by nominal GDP, which is the wrong way round.
This is the difference between nominal and real GDP, not an index number.
The ratio is right, but a price index is expressed with the base year equal to 100.

questions.prompt: Using Table 5, calculate (i) Kuva's real GDP in 2025 and (ii) the real GDP growth rate between 2024 and 2025.
hints: Use the deflator to turn nominal GDP into real GDP, then use the percentage change formula.
In the base year real and nominal GDP are equal; compare the two real figures and divide the change by the earlier year's value.
questions.targets: Real GDP from a deflator and real growth rate
marking_points: = 1,200 billion zed [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer converts 2025 GDP to 1,200 billion zed in 2024 prices and finds real growth of 20%.

questions.prompt: Tarn's GDP deflator rose from 125 in 2024 to 150 in 2025. By how much did the average price level rise?
hints: Use the percentage change formula applied to the two index numbers.
Find the change in the index, then divide by the value in the earlier year.
questions.targets: Percentage change between two index numbers

options.misconception: The index rose by 25 points, but a percentage change must be divided by the starting value.
150 is 50 above the base of 100, but that compares with the base year, not with 2024.
This divides the change by the new value (150) instead of the starting value (125).

questions.prompt: Using Table 6, calculate Veld's real GDP per capita in 2025.
hints: You need two steps: remove the effect of prices, then share output across the population.
Convert nominal GDP to real GDP with the deflator first, then divide by population, keeping the millions consistent.
questions.targets: Real GDP per capita in two steps
marking_points: Real GDP = (4,800 ÷ 120) × 100 = 4,000 million zed [1]
Real GDP per capita = 4,000 million ÷ 8 million [1]
= 500 zed per person [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer deflates GDP to 4,000 million zed and divides by 8 million to get 500 zed per person.

questions.prompt: Using Table 7, calculate Kuva's total nominal GDP in 2025.
hints: Use the per capita formula and rearrange it to find the total.
Combine the two figures and take care with the millions in the population.
questions.targets: Total GDP from a per capita figure
marking_points: GDP = GDP per capita × population = 2,500 × 12 million [1]
= 30,000 million zed (30 billion zed) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer multiplies per capita GDP by population to get 30,000 million (30 billion) zed.

questions.prompt: Using Table 8, what was Tarn's rate of economic growth in 2025?
hints: Use the percentage change formula for real GDP between two consecutive years.
Take the change from the previous year and divide by the previous year's value.
questions.targets: Annual real GDP growth rate

options.misconception: This is growth over two years (2023 to 2025), not growth in 2025.
Real GDP rose by 21 billion zed, but that is the absolute change, not a percentage.
This divides the change by the 2025 value instead of the 2024 value.

questions.prompt: Using Table 9, calculate the percentage change in Veld's real GDP per capita between Year 1 and Year 2.
hints: Use real GDP per capita for each year and the percentage change formula.
Work out output per person in each year first, then compare the two figures using the earlier year as the base.
questions.targets: Growth in real GDP per capita when population also grows
marking_points: Year 1 real GDP per capita = 500 ÷ 10 = 50 zed [1]
Year 2 real GDP per capita = 572 ÷ 11 = 52 zed [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer finds per capita values of 50 and 52 zed and a 4% rise (lower than the 14.4% rise in total real GDP).

questions.prompt: In Kuva, real GDP has been falling for several months and unemployment is rising. Which phase of the business cycle is Kuva most likely in?
hints: Use the four phases of the business cycle.
Match the direction of real GDP and unemployment in the scenario with the phase that has the same features.
questions.targets: Identifying business cycle phases

options.text: Expansion
options.misconception: The economy is changing, but in an expansion real GDP rises and unemployment falls.

options.text: Peak
options.misconception: A peak comes just before a fall, but at the peak real GDP is at its highest, not falling.

options.text: Contraction
Trough
options.misconception: Unemployment is high near a trough, but the trough is the lowest point where the fall ends, not a period of continued falling.

questions.prompt: Define the term recession.
hints: This term is linked to the contraction phase of the business cycle.
Your definition needs to say what happens to output and for how long.
questions.targets: Precise definition of recession
marking_points: A fall in real GDP [1]
for at least two consecutive quarters (six months) [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer refers to falling real GDP (not just slower growth) over at least two consecutive quarters.

questions.prompt: Veld's actual real GDP is above its potential output. Which of the following is most likely?
hints: Use the business cycle diagram with the long-term growth trend (potential output).
Think about what producing beyond normal capacity means for the use of labour and for prices.
questions.targets: Positive output gap

options.text: There is a deflationary (recessionary) gap and high unemployment
options.misconception: Output gaps are linked to unemployment, but this gap occurs when output is below potential.

options.text: There is an inflationary gap, with unemployment below its natural rate and upward pressure on prices
The long-term growth trend has shifted downwards
options.misconception: Actual and potential output differ, but the trend reflects long-run capacity, not short-run fluctuations.

options.text: The economy is at a trough
options.misconception: A trough is a turning point, but there actual output is well below potential.

questions.prompt: Using Table 10, at the end of which quarter was Tarn's real GDP at its lowest level (the trough)?
hints: A growth rate shows the direction in which real GDP is moving, not its level.
Find the last quarter in which real GDP fell before it began to rise again.
questions.targets: Reading a trough from growth-rate data

table.caption: Table 10: Quarterly real GDP growth in Tarn

options.text: Q2
options.misconception: Growth slowed sharply in Q2, but real GDP was still rising.

options.text: Q3
options.misconception: Growth first turned negative in Q3, but real GDP kept falling in Q4.

options.text: Q5
options.misconception: Growth turned positive in Q5, which means real GDP had already started to rise.

options.text: Q4

questions.prompt: On a business cycle diagram, real GDP in Kuva is shown below the long-term growth trend line. Explain what this shows about Kuva's economy.
hints: The trend line on this diagram represents potential output.
Compare actual with potential output, then consider what that means for the use of labour and other resources, and for prices.
questions.targets: Negative output gap on the business cycle diagram
marking_points: Actual output is below potential output, so there is a negative (deflationary/recessionary) output gap [1]
Resources are not fully used, so unemployment is above its natural rate [1]
The economy is likely in a contraction or near a trough, with little upward pressure on the price level [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer names the negative output gap, links it to unemployed resources, and places the economy in the contraction/trough part of the cycle.

questions.prompt: Why are GDP per capita figures often converted using purchasing power parity (PPP) exchange rates when comparing countries?
hints: Think about purchasing power parity and what a market exchange rate does and does not reflect.
Consider why the same income, converted at market exchange rates, might buy far more in one country than in another.
questions.targets: Rationale for PPP adjustment

options.text: To allow for differences in the cost of living, so that each figure reflects what incomes can actually buy
To remove the effect of inflation over time within each country
options.misconception: This is an adjustment, but it is what converting nominal to real values does.

options.text: To include the value of non-marketed output such as housework
options.misconception: GDP does miss this output, but PPP does not add anything to measured output.

options.text: To divide output by the size of each country's population
options.misconception: This is the per capita adjustment, which is made before any PPP conversion.

questions.prompt: Define the term informal economy.
hints: This term matters when judging how accurate official GDP figures are.
A full definition covers what kind of activity it is and how it relates to official records.
questions.targets: Precise definition of the informal economy
marking_points: Economic activity (legal or illegal) that is not registered, regulated or taxed by the government [1]
so it is not recorded in official national income statistics such as GDP [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer describes unregistered, untaxed activity and states that it is left out of official GDP.

questions.prompt: Explain two reasons why GDP per capita may not be an accurate measure of well-being in a country such as Veld.
hints: Consider what GDP per capita counts and what it leaves out.
For each reason, name the limitation and then show how GDP per capita could change without well-being changing in the same way.
questions.targets: Limitations of GDP per capita as a well-being measure
marking_points: First limitation identified, e.g. GDP per capita says nothing about how income is distributed [1]
Explained, e.g. average income can rise while most people's incomes stay the same, so many are not better off [1]
Second limitation identified, e.g. GDP ignores environmental damage, non-marketed output, leisure or product quality [1]
Explained, e.g. output that pollutes raises GDP while harming health and quality of life [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer gives two different limitations and, for each, explains how GDP per capita and well-being can move apart.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the data in Table 11?
hints: Read each column carefully and note which figures are per person rather than totals.
Check each statement against the numbers, and reject any that needs information the table does not give.
questions.targets: Interpreting multiple development indicators

table.caption: Table 11: Selected indicators for three countries, 2025

options.text: Kuva must have the lowest well-being because it has the lowest income per person
options.misconception: Income matters, but Kuva has high life expectancy and a small footprint, so well-being cannot be judged from income alone.

options.text: Veld has the highest income per person but also the largest environmental impact per person
Tarn has a higher life expectancy than Kuva
options.misconception: This misreads the table: Tarn's life expectancy (70) is lower than Kuva's (78).

options.text: Veld has the largest total national income of the three countries
options.misconception: Veld's per capita figure is highest, but total income also depends on population, which is not given.

questions.prompt: Using Table 11, explain why Kuva might rank above Veld on the Happy Planet Index (HPI) even though its GNI per capita is much lower.
hints: Use the components of the Happy Planet Index and how they are combined.
Compare the two countries on each component shown in the table, and note which component pulls the index down as it rises.
questions.targets: How the HPI differs from income-based rankings

table.caption: Table 11: Selected indicators for three countries, 2025

marking_points: The HPI combines well-being and life expectancy and adjusts for ecological footprint; income is not directly included [1]
Kuva's life expectancy (78 years) is close to Veld's (80 years) [1]
Kuva's ecological footprint (2.0) is much smaller than Veld's (7.0), so it achieves similar outcomes with far less environmental impact, which raises its HPI [1]
questions.model_answer_note: A full-mark answer explains that income is not in the HPI and uses the life expectancy and footprint data to show Kuva's advantage.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would raise Veld's measured GDP but could reduce the well-being of its people?
hints: Think about what is counted in GDP and which effects on people it ignores.
For each option, first ask whether measured GDP rises, then ask whether people could be worse off.
questions.targets: GDP rising while well-being falls

options.text: More people doing unpaid volunteer work
options.misconception: This changes how people use their time, but unpaid work is not counted in GDP.

options.text: Workers choosing to take more leisure time
options.misconception: This affects well-being, but more leisure usually lowers measured output rather than raising it.

options.text: A new factory increases output but also increases air pollution
Mobile phones improve in quality while their prices stay the same
options.misconception: This is a change in goods, but GDP does not capture quality improvements at unchanged prices, and people are better off.
